text.p: The international tribunal on Rwanda's 1994 genocide reopened on Thursday with former government official Jean-Paul Akayesu in the dock, charged with genocide and crimes against humanity.
Akayesu's defence lawyer, Nicolas Taingaye from the Central African Republic, told reporters that his team would vigorously test the credibility of some 31 prosecution witnesses.

Akayesu, 43, a Hutu former mayor in central Rwanda's Taba commune, has pleaded not guilty to the charges. The prosecution says the crimes were committed between April and June 1994 when an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.
Wearing a light blue suit, Akayesu appeared relaxed when he was brought to court before a panel of three judges under tight security. He faces life imprisonment if convicted.
Taingaye, one of Akayesu's three lawyers, said: "The strategy of the defence will be to verify the credibility or the absence of credibility of prosecution witnesses."
He said he expected cross-examination of the 31 witnesses to last six weeks. Two women and one man, all Rwandans, will be the first to testify on Thursday.
In a major boost for the tribunal dogged by delays and allegations of mismanagement, officials said a deal had been signed with Cameroon for the transfer of four leading suspects held there.

Tribunal spokeswoman Beatrice Lacoste told reporters before Akayesu's trial opened that authority had been obtained to transfer Theoneste Bagosora, a former senior army official, and three others to tribunal headquarters in Tanzania.
"We have been negotiating with the government of Cameroon to tranfer these four indicted persons to detention in Arusha," said Lacoste.
"The agreement has been signed and they will be transferred to Arusha," she added without giving details.
Bagosora is a former director of cabinet in the ministry of defence and was effectively running the tiny central African nation in the president's absence at the time of the genocide.
He first fled to neighbouring Zaire and then to Cameroon as an international manhunt for his arrest was stepped up in 1995.

Twenty-one people have been indicted by the tribunal including Akayesu. Eight suspects are still at large, seven are held in Arusha including Akayesu, four are in detention in Cameroon and the United States and Switzerland hold one each.
The suspects are all accused of crimes committed during the genocide in Rwanda sparked off by the assassination of Hutu president and military strongman Juvenal Habyarimana.

Angry Hutu mobs, militia and soldiers took up arms and hunted down Tutsis and moderate Hutus opposed to Habyarimana's military junta. The mass slaughter ended after victorious Tutsi rebels took power and drove the Hutus into exile.
Akayesu's trial was adjourned last October to allow the defence time to prepare its case.
The U.N. tribunal had a series of false starts in 1995 with adjournments on procedural grounds.

But far worse for its image was the disclosure last October that U.N. headquarters in New York had sent auditors and investigators to probe the tribunal in Arusha and its prosecution office in Kigali, the Rwandan capital. Details of the inquiry were not made public but were linked to allegations of mismanagement.
